claims.text: Captured drill output: alert pending then firing with both shares above 6.7%; after the revert, inactive with the 5-minute share below and the 1-hour share still above 6.7%. percent() prints the 6.72% threshold with one decimal.

An alert resolves when its expression returns no result; with `A and B`, the expression returns nothing once either side is false, so the alert resolves when the 5-minute share falls even if the 1-hour share is still above.

claims.text: A revert restores manifests, not data: an applied migration stays, so the older api runs against the newer schema.

claims.text: Mitigate first (revert a recent change) when a change to the api's environment landed shortly before the alert; find the cause first when nothing changed or a revert cannot undo the change; trying fixes as ideas come rarely fits.

A runbook with first safe steps for one alert fits when anyone in the rotation may be paged; a list of every cause fits only as a reference for later study; no runbook fits only when one person built and runs everything.

Choices: no change + 503 -> replicas by commit after checking connections; applied migration -> revert only if it added tables or columns the older api can ignore (nullable or with a default), else escalate; canary in progress -> weight 0 first, watch the 5-minute share.

claims.text: A runbook step nobody has run since the system changed may fail during an incident; running it in a drill on staging finds that out first.

Try it: grep finds `runbook:` at lines 32, 62, 90, 118 of slo.rules.yml naming product-reads-burn.md, order-placement-burn.md, order-placement-latency-burn.md, refund-requests-burn.md, the four files in docs/runbooks/.
The catalog-reads concurrency limit comes from the bulkhead lesson; canary-steps --bad gives the canary the same one-at-a-time limit.
In a Prometheus alerting rule, labels identify the alert (alerts are told apart by their label set), while annotations hold informational text for people, such as a description or a runbook link.
